OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $A$ be an infinite sequence of integers such that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. How fast must $A$ grow?
#1103: [Er81h,p.180]
number theory
Erdős notes there exists such a sequence which grows exponentially, but does not expect such a sequence of polynomial growth.
In [Er81h] he asked whether there is an infinite sequence of integers $A$ such that, for every $a\in A$ and prime $p$, if\[a\equiv t\pmod{p^2}\]then $1\leq t<p^2/2$. He noted that such a sequence has the property that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. He wrote 'I am doubtful if such a sequence exists. I formulated this problem while writing these lines and must ask the indulgence of the reader if it turns out to be trivial.'
Indeed, there are trivially at most finitely many such $a$, since there cannot be any primes $p\in (a^{1/2},(2a)^{1/2}]$, but there exist primes in $(x,\sqrt{2}x)$ for all large $x$.
If $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ is such a sequence then van Doorn and Tao [vDTa25] have shown that $a_j > 0.24j^{4/3}$ for all $j$, and further that there exists such a sequence (furthermore with squarefree terms) such that\[a_j < \exp(5j/\log j)\]for all large $j$. A superior lower bound of $a_j \gg j^{15/11-o(1)}$ had earlier been found by Konyagin [Ko04] when considering the finite case [1109].
They also obtain further results for the generalisation from squarefree to $k$-free integers, and also replacing $A+A$ with $A\cup (A+A)\cup(A+A+A)$. 
See also [1109] for the finite analogue of this problem.
Additional thanks to: Benjamin Bedert, Terence Tao, and Wouter van Doorn

 The paper Terence Tao and I just uploaded is mostly aimed at resolving #1102, but we have some results for this problem as well. In particular, we improve upon the $0$ density result in my earlier comment and, in the other direction, we show the existence of a sequence with sub-exponential growth. More precisely, define $\mathcal{SF} \subset \mathbb{N}$ to be the set of squarefree integers, let $kA$ be the set of $k$ (not necessarily distinct) elements of $A$, and let us say that $A$ has squarefree sums if $2A \subset \mathcal{SF}$. We then have the following results:
Theorem 1. For any sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \} \subset \mathbb{N}$ with squarefree sums, we have $a_j > 0.24j^{4/3}$ for all $j \in \mathbb{N}$.
Theorem 2. There exists a sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \} \subset \mathcal{SF}$ with squarefree sums for which $a_j < \exp(5j / \log j)$ holds for all large enough $j \in \mathbb{N}$.
We furthermore observe that the proofs of Theorem 1 and 2 can be modified to obtain the following two bonus results on $k$-free sums and sums of three elements respectively:
Theorem 3. For any $k \ge 2$ and any sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \} \subset \mathbb{N}$ with $k$-free sums, we have $a_j \gg j^{2k/(2k-1)}$ for all $j \in \mathbb{N}$.
Theorem 4. There exists an absolute constant $C$ and a sequence $A = \{a_1 < a_2 < \cdots \}$ with $A \cup 2A \cup 3A \subset \mathcal{SF}$ for which $a_j < \exp(Cj^2 / \log j)$ holds for all $j \in \mathbb{N}$.
Note that Theorem 4 can not be extended to sums of four elements, as $4A$ of course contains elements divisible by $4$, if $A$ is non-empty.
EDIT: Some of our results have turned out to be obsolete by the results from Konyagin mentioned below, so Terry and I rewrote the relevant parts of our paper. The original arXiv version containing proofs of the above theorems can be found here.

 Benjamin Bedert has pointed out to us that there is in fact a significant body of literature on this problem already, namely
* P. Erdős and A. Sárközy. On divisibility properties of integers of the form a + a′. Acta Math. Hungar., 50(1-
2):117–122, 1987. doi:10.1007/BF01903370.
* S. V. Konyagin. Problems of the set of square-free numbers. Izv. Ross. Akad. Nauk Ser. Mat., 68(3):63–90, 2004.
doi:10.1070/IM2004v068n03ABEH000486.
* G. N. Sárközy. On a problem of P. Erdős. Acta Math. Hungar., 60(3-4):271–282, 1992. doi:10.1007/BF00051645.
* Katalin Gyarmati. On divisibility properties of integers of the form ab + 1. Period. Math. Hungar., 43(1-2):71–79,
2001. doi:10.1023/A:1015229531017.
In particular, the results of Konyagin give the improved lower bound
$$ a_j \gg j^{15/11} \exp\left( -O\left(\frac{\log j}{\sqrt{\log\log j}} \right)\right).$$
Konyagin also constructs subsets of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with squarefree sums of cardinality $\gg \log^2 N \log\log N$. If there was a way to paste these constructions together for various $N$, this would give an example with
$$ a_j \ll \exp( O( j^{1/2} / \log^{1/2} j ))$$
for all $j$, but we have not checked whether such a pasting is possible.

 For a prime $p$, let $A_p$ be the set of residue classes $x \pmod{p^2}$ for which at least two distinct $a \in A$ exist with $a \equiv x \pmod{p^2}$. Then $|A_p| < \frac{p^2}{2}$ for all $p$ by the assumption that $A + A$ only contains squarefree integers. Taking the product $M = (p_1p_2 \cdots p_k)^2$ of distinct primes $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$ then gives that the number of residue classes $x \pmod{M}$ that occur more than once among the $a \in A$ is smaller than $\frac{M}{2^k}$. By the infinitude of primes we therefore obtain $A \cap \{1, 2, \ldots, x\} = o(x)$.
I understand that this is a terrible bound which is clearly improvable, but hey, you have to start somewhere!

A partial proof 
claimed by Xiyu Hu (using GPT-5.6 Sol).
 Summary:
 I would like to share a partial result toward Erdős Problem #1103.The construction follows the general line of ideas developed by Wouter van Doorn and Terence Tao in their paper Growth rates of sequences governed by the squarefree properties of its translates, particularly their CRT-based treatment of local obstructions and iterative approach to constructing sequences with squarefree sums. The additional ingredient here is a more refined use of Konyagin’s quadratic Brun sieve in the finite extension step, which leads to the logarithmic-square bound above. I prove that there exists an infinite set \(A\subset\mathbb N\) such that all pairwise sums, including diagonal sums, are squarefree and\[
 |A\cap[1,x]|\gg(\log x)^2.
\]Equivalently, if \(A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\), then \(a_j\leq\exp(C\sqrt j)\).
 Notes:
 The proof combines a compatible Chinese-remainder class for the small prime-square obstructions with a Konyagin-style quadratic Brun sieve for the remaining primes, followed by iteration of a finite extension principle. The optimal asymptotic growth in Erdős Problem #1103 remains open.
An arXiv submission is planned.
